sources.cite: Gollwitzer, P. M. (1999). Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans. American Psychologist, 54, 493-503.
sources.design: narrative review introducing construct + early experiments
sources.effect: n/a
sources.finding_quote: Implementation intentions delegate control of goal-directed responses to anticipated situational cues, which automatically elicit these responses when encountered (search synthesis; full text not independently fetched).

sources.cite: Gollwitzer, P. M. & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69-119.
sources.finding_quote: Findings from 94 independent tests showed that implementation intentions had a positive effect of medium-to-large magnitude (d = .65) on goal attainment.

sources.cite: Adriaanse, M. A., Vinkers, C. D. W., De Ridder, D. T. D., Hox, J. J. & De Wit, J. B. F. (2011). Do implementation intentions help to eat a healthy diet? A systematic review and meta-analysis of the empirical evidence. Appetite, 56(1), 183-193.
sources.effect: d = 0.51 (healthy eating); d = 0.29 (unhealthy eating)
sources.finding_quote: implementation intentions to be effective in both promoting healthy eating (d=0.51) as well as decreasing unhealthy eating (d=0.29)

sources.cite: Milkman, K. L., Beshears, J., Choi, J. J., Laibson, D. & Madrian, B. C. (2011). Using implementation intentions prompts to enhance influenza vaccination rates. PNAS, 108(26), 10415-10420.
sources.design: large field experiment, employer vaccination clinics
sources.effect: control 33.1% vaccinated; date-only prompt +1.5 percentage points
sources.finding_quote: the vaccination rate among control condition employees at 33.1%, and employees who received the prompt to write down just a date having a vaccination rate 1.5 percentage points higher than the control group

backfire.cite: Dalton, A. N. & Spiller, S. A. (2012). Too Much of a Good Thing: The Benefits of Implementation Intentions Depend on the Number of Goals. Journal of Consumer Research, 39(3), 600-614.
backfire.condition: Implementation intentions for multiple simultaneous goals draw attention to execution difficulty, undermine commitment, and reverse the single-goal benefit.

unverified.cite: "Rigid plans fail when the cue never occurs" — no dedicated empirical citation located.
unverified.reason: Searched; discussed qualitatively in review literature as a boundary condition but no specific study verified this session.

sources.cite: Gollwitzer, P. M., Sheeran, P., Michalski, V. & Seifert, A. E. (2009). When Intentions Go Public: Does Social Reality Widen the Intention-Behavior Gap? Psychological Science, 20(5), 612-618.
sources.effect: reduced 1-week persistence (field); fewer opportunities seized (lab); held for strong but not weak identity commitment
sources.finding_quote: Identity-related behavioral intentions that had been noticed by other people were translated into action less intensively than those that had been ignored (Studies 1-3) ... it held among participants with strong but not weak commitment to the identity goal (Study 3).

backfire.cite: Hollenbeck, J. R., Williams, C. R. & Klein, H. J. (1989). An empirical examination of the antecedents of commitment to difficult goals. Journal of Applied Psychology, 74(1), 18-23.
backfire.condition: Public statement of a goal (vs. private) was associated with higher, not lower, goal commitment — opposite direction from the intention-announcement claim.

backfire.cite: Klein, H. J., Wesson, M. J., Hollenbeck, J. R. & Alge, B. J. (1999). Goal commitment and the goal-setting process: Conceptual clarification and empirical synthesis. Journal of Applied Psychology, 84(6), 885-896.
backfire.condition: Meta-analysis of 83 independent samples; public declaration of a goal is one antecedent that generally strengthens (not weakens) goal commitment.

unverified.cite: Wicklund, R. A. & Gollwitzer, P. M. (1982). Symbolic Self-Completion.
unverified.reason: Theory book, pre-DOI era; no ISBN confirmed in this session.

unverified.cite: Klein, H. J., Cooper, J. T. & Monahan, C. A. (2013). Goal Commitment. In Locke & Latham (Eds.), New Developments in Goal Setting and Task Performance (pp. 65-89). Routledge.
unverified.reason: Lead confirmed to exist via search, but only the edited volume's own DOI (10.4324/9780203082744, resolving to editor "Locke") was found in Crossref; no chapter-level DOI resolves to these chapter authors, so it fails the title/author match check.

unverified.cite: Pre-registered replication of Gollwitzer et al. 2009.
unverified.reason: Searched; none found in this session.

sources.cite: Oettingen, G., Pak, H. & Schnetter, K. (2001). Self-regulation of goal-setting: Turning free fantasies about the future into binding goals. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 80(5), 736-753.
sources.effect: future-then-reality order produced expectancy-dependent commitment; other orders did not
sources.finding_quote: future-then-reality produces selective expectancy-driven commitment, reality-then-future produces no contrast effect, and neither alone (Indulging or Dwelling) produces it.

sources.cite: Wang, G., Wang, Y. & Gai, X. (2021). A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Mental Contrasting With Implementation Intentions on Goal Attainment. Frontiers in Psychology, 12, 565202.
sources.design: meta-analysis, k=24 effect sizes / 21 studies, N=15,907
sources.finding_quote: Results showed that MCII to be effective for goal attainment with a small to medium effect size (g = 0.336). The effect was mainly moderated by intervention style.

backfire.cite: Kappes, H. B. & Oettingen, G. (2011). Positive fantasies about idealized futures sap energy. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 47(4), 719-729.
backfire.condition: Induced positive fantasies (contrasting without the obstacle/plan step) reduced energy and effort relative to fantasies that questioned the future, negative fantasies, or neutral fantasies.

sources.cite: Buehler, R., Griffin, D. & Ross, M. (1994). Exploring the "planning fallacy": Why people underestimate their task completion times. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 67(3), 366-381.
sources.design: field/lab study of thesis completion predictions
sources.effect: mean predicted 33.9 days vs. actual 55.5 days; ~30% finished by their predicted date
sources.finding_quote: the average estimate was 33.9 days [predicted] ... only about 30% of the students completed the project on the timeline they had predicted [actual mean 55.5 days].

sources.cite: Kruger, J. & Evans, M. (2004). If you don't want to be late, enumerate: Unpacking reduces the planning fallacy. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 40, 586-598.
sources.design: multiple experiments (holiday shopping, getting ready, formatting, food prep)
sources.effect: unpacking into components produced significantly longer, more realistic time estimates
sources.finding_quote: participants in the unpack condition estimated significantly longer time [for tasks such as holiday shopping].

sources.cite: Forsyth, D. K. & Burt, C. D. B. (2008). Allocating time to future tasks: The effect of task segmentation on planning fallacy bias. Memory & Cognition, 36(4), 791-798.
sources.effect: summed subtask time estimates exceeded single-task estimate ("segmentation effect")
sources.finding_quote: allocated time for a single task was significantly smaller than the summed time allocated to the individual subtasks.

sources.cite: Buehler, R., Griffin, D. & Peetz, J. (2010). The Planning Fallacy: Cognitive, Motivational, and Social Origins. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 43, 1-62.
sources.effect: n/a
sources.finding_quote: Reviews the definition, controversies, and scope of empirical research documenting the planning fallacy (search synthesis; not independently fetched in full).

backfire.cite: Buehler, R. & Griffin, D. (2003). Planning, personality, and prediction: The role of future focus in optimistic time predictions. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 92, 80-90.
backfire.condition: Instructing a detailed, narrative, future-focused completion scenario ("a complete picture, from beginning to end, of how this assignment" will proceed) increased optimistic bias rather than reducing it — a different manipulation from itemized unpacking, and a boundary condition worth naming against Timeline's design.

unverified.cite: Evidence that explicitly sequencing steps/prerequisites (critical-path style) improves plan execution.
unverified.reason: Searched (unpacking + planning fallacy + critical path + prerequisite sequencing combinations); none found. The claim's evidence base supports unpacking for estimation, not sequencing for execution.

sources.cite: Bryan, J. F. & Locke, E. A. (1967). Parkinson's Law as a goal-setting phenomenon. Organizational Behavior & Human Performance, 2, 258-275.
sources.effect: generous deadlines led to lower self-set performance goals, which in turn drove slower work
sources.finding_quote: People given generous deadlines set lower performance goals for themselves, and those lower goals, not the time itself, drove the slower pace (search synthesis).

sources.cite: Ordóñez, L. & Benson, L. III (1997). Decisions under Time Pressure: How Time Constraint Affects Risky Decision Making. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 71, 121-140.
sources.effect: time-constrained decision makers shifted toward simplifying/eliminating strategies
sources.finding_quote: decision makers tend to focus on screening items out of the choice set when making a decision under a time constraint in order to reduce the set and thus the processing time necessary to make a final choice (search synthesis).

sources.cite: Edland, A. & Svenson, O. (1993). Judgment and Decision Making Under Time Pressure. In Svenson & Maule (Eds.), Time Pressure and Stress in Human Judgment and Decision Making.
sources.design: narrative review of ~3 decades of studies
sources.effect: n/a
sources.finding_quote: effects of time pressure include an over-reliance on negative information and an increased reliance on fewer attributes or dimensions in making choices (search synthesis).

replication.cite: Hyndman, K. & Bisin, A. (2026). Replication of "Procrastination, Deadlines, and Performance: Self-Control by Precommitment". Psychological Science.

backfire.cite: RETRACTED: Ariely, D. & Wertenbroch, K. (2002). Procrastination, Deadlines, and Performance: Self-Control by Precommitment. Psychological Science, 13(3).
backfire.condition: Retracted September 2026 (retraction DOI 10.1177/09567976261488042) after a failed large replication (Hyndman & Bisin 2026, n roughly 2x+ original) and forensic evidence (Data Colada) that the original Study 2 data were tampered with or fabricated. Per §6.2 tie-break rule 1, this source must not be used as supporting evidence for timeboxing; it was the primary basis for the brief's own question about self- vs. externally-imposed deadlines, and that basis no longer stands.

backfire.cite: Edland, A. & Svenson, O. (1993) and Ordóñez, L. & Benson, L. III (1997), as above.
backfire.condition: Both describe time pressure degrading decision process quality (fewer attributes considered, over-weighting of negative information), in tension with the claim's assertion of "no loss of decision quality for convergent tasks."

unverified.cite: Parkinson, C. N. (1955). Parkinson's Law. The Economist.
unverified.reason: Magazine essay, not an empirical study; no DOI exists. Practitioner/practice source (type practice).

sources.cite: Wilson, K. & Korn, J. H. (2007). Attention during Lectures: Beyond Ten Minutes. Teaching of Psychology, 34, 85-89.
sources.design: review of note-taking, observational, self-report and physiological studies
sources.effect: n/a
sources.finding_quote: the research on which this estimate is based provides little support for the belief that students' attention declines after 10 to 15 minutes. Most studies failed to account for individual differences in attention.

sources.cite: Bradbury, N. (2016). Attention span during lectures: 8 seconds, 10 minutes, or more? Advances in Physiology Education, 40(4), 509-513.
sources.effect: n/a
sources.finding_quote: The available primary data do not support the concept of a 10- to 15-minute attention limit. The 15-minute attention span is a myth.

sources.cite: Mackworth, N. H. (1948). The Breakdown of Vigilance during Prolonged Visual Search. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1, 6-21.
sources.effect: detection declined ~10-15% in the first 30 minutes, then more gradually over the remaining 90 minutes
sources.finding_quote: Mackworth's results indicated a decline in signal detection over time, known as a vigilance decrement (search synthesis); paradigm is passive sustained monitoring, analogical at best to self-paced writing.

sources.cite: Warm, J. S., Parasuraman, R. & Matthews, G. (2008). Vigilance Requires Hard Mental Work and Is Stressful. Human Factors, 50(3), 433-441.
sources.design: review across task type, workload, neural, and stress evidence
sources.effect: n/a
sources.finding_quote: the workload of vigilance is high and sensitive to factors that increase processing demands (search synthesis), challenging the view that vigilance decrement reflects mere understimulation.

replication.cite: Hagger, M. S. et al. (2016). A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(4), 546-573.
Vohs, K. D. et al. (2021). A Multisite Preregistered Paradigmatic Test of the Ego-Depletion Effect. Psychological Science.

sources.cite: Harkin, B., Webb, T. L., Chang, B. P. I., Prestwich, A., Conner, M., Kellar, I., Benn, Y. & Sheeran, P. (2016). Does monitoring goal progress promote goal attainment? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence. Psychological Bulletin, 142(2), 198-229.
sources.effect: d approx 0.40 (medium) on goal attainment
sources.finding_quote: a reliable medium-sized effect (d approx 0.40) on goal attainment was found across health, money and other domains ... monitoring helped more when progress was physically recorded rather than just noticed, and it helped more when the information was made visible or reported rather than kept in your head (search synthesis).

sources.cite: Michie, S., Abraham, C., Whittington, C., McAteer, J. & Gupta, S. (2009). Effective techniques in healthy eating and physical activity interventions: A meta-regression. Health Psychology, 28(6), 690-701.
sources.effect: self-monitoring among the most consistently effective techniques
sources.finding_quote: the technique of self-monitoring was effective and its effect was increased in combination with other techniques theoretically predicted to increase effectiveness (search synthesis).

sources.cite: Burke, L. E., Wang, J. & Sevick, M. A. (2011). Self-Monitoring in Weight Loss: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Journal of the American Dietetic Association, 111(1), 92-102.
sources.effect: dietary self-monitoring associated with greater weight loss; dose-response with consistency
sources.finding_quote: dietary self-monitoring was significantly associated with weight loss, and ... weight loss was significantly greater among individuals who returned self-monitoring logs on a more consistent basis (search synthesis).

backfire.cite: Deci, E. L., Koestner, R. & Ryan, R. M. (1999). A meta-analytic review of experiments examining the effects of extrinsic rewards on intrinsic motivation. Psychological Bulletin, 125(6), 627-668.
backfire.condition: Engagement-, completion-, and performance-contingent rewards significantly undermined free-choice intrinsic motivation (d = -0.40, -0.36, -0.28); relevant when monitoring is paired with an extrinsic reward/target rather than kept reward-free.

backfire.cite: Lepper, M. R., Greene, D. & Nisbett, R. E. (1973). Undermining children's intrinsic interest with extrinsic reward: A test of the "overjustification" hypothesis. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 28(1), 129-137.
backfire.condition: Classic overjustification effect: expected extrinsic reward for an already-interesting activity reduced subsequent free-choice engagement.

unverified.cite: Does monitoring become a gamed (Goodhart-style) target, or does poor recorded progress cause discouragement/abandonment, in personal (reward-free) self-monitoring specifically?
unverified.reason: Searched; no direct empirical test of this specific framing found. Deci/Lepper concern reward-contingent monitoring, an adjacent but not identical question.

sources.cite: Goethals, G. R. & Reckman, R. F. (1973). The perception of consistency in attitudes. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 9, 491-501.
sources.effect: attitude-changers distorted recalled pre-discussion attitude toward new attitude; controls did not
sources.finding_quote: subjects distorted their recall of their initial stand on bussing so as to make it consistent with their new attitude ... control subjects did not distort their original bussing attitudes.

sources.cite: Ross, M. (1989). Relation of Implicit Theories to the Construction of Personal Histories. Psychological Review, 96(2), 341-357.
sources.effect: n/a
sources.finding_quote: people possess implicit theories regarding the inherent consistency of their attributes ... implicit theories of stability and change can lead to biases in recall.

sources.cite: Conway, M. & Ross, M. (1984). Getting what you want by revising what you had. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 47(4), 738-748.
sources.design: field experiment: study-skills program with pre/post self-ratings
sources.effect: recalled baseline self-ratings revised downward to manufacture illusory improvement
sources.finding_quote: asked individuals to evaluate their study skills before participating in a study skills program, and at the conclusion of the program, participants were asked to recall their original ratings ... participants nevertheless perceived an improvement in their study skills (search synthesis) although the program was in fact ineffective.

sources.cite: Wolfe, M. B. & Williams, T. J. (2018). Poor metacognitive awareness of belief change. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 71(9), 1898-1910.
sources.design: 2 experiments (beliefs about spanking, pre/post persuasive text)
sources.effect: recalled initial beliefs biased toward current beliefs; poor awareness of belief change
sources.finding_quote: Belief recollections were closer to current beliefs than they were to initial beliefs, which suggests that people have poor metacognitive awareness of changes in their beliefs.

unverified.cite: Visible prior ratings anchor subsequent self-ratings and suppress real change; hiding the prior rating reduces (but does not eliminate) the anchoring.
unverified.reason: Found only as secondary/synthesized commentary (e.g., discussion of performance-review anchoring) in this session, not as a primary source fetched and read directly; no specific citation could be verified. Relevant to whether scoresheet should hide the "before" column.
